title: What Forbade You Folly Has Forbidden You
intro: An elegy by Baha' al-Din Zuhayr. E. H. Palmer's Cambridge edition of his diwan heads it as a lament for his son, and so, the Cairo editors report, does the Beirut edition; the Cairo edition of al-Jabalawi and Abu al-Fadl Ibrahim heads it only as an elegy for someone dear to him. It opens with the poet scolding his own heart, which has had its fill of love and, now that morning has come, finds nothing to praise in its long night journey through youth. Then he turns to the one he has lost and reproaches him as a lover would, for a long desertion he was never used to, until he admits that death, not choice, took him, blames himself for staying alive, and ends at the grave, praying for rain on it and sending a greeting of peace on the breeze. Ahmad al-Hashimi chose eleven of its lines for the elegies in his anthology Jawahir al-Adab.

translation: Whatever forbade you folly has forbidden you,
and you have tasted enough of passion.
1.sharh: The poet speaks to his own heart: something too grave to name has cured it of folly, and it has had its fill of love. The lines that follow show that the thing is a death.

translation: Long was your night journey through the night of youthful play,
and now it is morning, and you do not praise the journey.
2.sharh: His youth was a long night march through pleasure, and now that morning has come he finds nothing in it to praise. The line turns an Arabic proverb around: travellers praise the night's march when morning comes.

translation: Do not despair at what the nights bring,
and tell me, if you despair, what can you do?
3.sharh: He tells himself not to give in to grief at what time has brought, since grief achieves nothing and cannot undo what has happened.

translation: How can you blame a blow of fate, when in it
it became clear who loved you and who hated you?
4.sharh: There is no point blaming the calamity: it is the very thing that showed him who truly loved him and who did not.

translation: My soul for the one over whom my soul melts away.
Taste, my heart, what your own hands have done.
5.sharh: He would give his life for the one he mourns, then turns on his heart: it chose to love, and now it must taste what it brought on itself. The words echo the Qur'an's “that is for what your hands have sent ahead” (22:10).

translation: By my life, you had no need of this,
and you could not tell your error from your right way.
6.sharh: He swears that his heart never needed this attachment, but it could not tell where it was going wrong, and so it rushed in.

translation: I have wasted away from love and been wretched with it,
while you answer every passion that calls you.
7.sharh: Love has worn him out and made him miserable, yet his heart still answers every love that calls it. The line sets the suffering self against the heart that keeps leading it on.

translation: Leave, my heart, what you were caught up in.
Do you not see your beloved has turned from you?
8.sharh: He tells his heart to give up its old ways, for the beloved has turned away from it. “Turned away” is the language of lovers; what has really happened is a death.

translation: Because of him my soul has risen to my collarbones,
and because of him my eye has looked upon death.
9.sharh: Grief for the one he loved brought him to the edge of death; because of him he has looked his own death in the face. The soul reaching the collarbones is the Qur'an's image of the last breath (75:26).

translation: O you who have gone from me, though you are my soul,
how can I bear to be parted from my soul?
10.sharh: He calls to the one who has gone, who was his very soul. No one can bear to be parted from his own soul, and that is what has happened to him.

translation: My beloved, how could you go away from me?
Do you know of anyone I have but you?
11.sharh: He reproaches the dead one for leaving, as a lover reproaches: he had no one else in his life, and the one he loved knew it.

translation: I see you have left me, and for a long time,
and you never accustomed me to that before.
12.sharh: He calls the death a desertion and complains of it as a lover would: a long absence, from one who had never stayed away before. Behind the complaint is the loss.

translation: I knew you could not bear to be without me,
and in loving me you defied whoever forbade you.
13.sharh: The one he lost could never bear to be apart from him, and in loving him ignored everyone who objected. That is why this long absence seems so strange.

translation: So how did those ways of yours change,
and who is this who has turned you from me?
14.sharh: He wonders what changed that loving nature, and who turned the beloved away from him, still speaking as if the parting were a choice.

translation: No, by God, you have offered no excuse,
and all people may be excused but you.
15.sharh: He swears that the beloved has given no excuse for leaving, and that he would excuse anyone but him. Another text reads “betrayal”: he never tried to betray, though everyone else betrays.

translation: You did not leave me of your own will,
but death struck you with what it struck.
16.sharh: Now he drops the reproach: the beloved did not leave by choice; death struck him. Leaving the blow unnamed makes it larger, as in the Qur'an's “there covered them of the sea what covered them” (20:78).

translation: If only you had stayed, for the sake of my frailty,
and all the people had been your ransom.
17.sharh: He wishes the one he lost had lived to support him in his weakness, and that everyone else had died in his place.

translation: It is hard for me, when I turn my eyes
searching for your place, not to see you.
18.sharh: Out of habit his eyes still search the place where the loved one used to be, and each time it is empty. That emptiness is what he finds hard to bear.

translation: I have not seen in anyone else, nor do I see,
your lovely ways or your graces.
19.sharh: He has never found the dead one's fine character and looks in anyone else, and he does not find them now: no one can take his place.

translation: I have sealed your love inside my heart,
and there it stays, still sealed.
20.sharh: He has sealed his love inside his heart, as a letter is sealed, so that nothing enters or leaves it, and there it stays untouched.

translation: Oh, my grief for your body, how it wastes,
and your radiance passes after its bloom.
21.sharh: He grieves for the body decaying in the grave, and for the light of the face, gone with the bloom that was in it.

translation: What right have I to claim I am faithful,
when I do not share your trial?
22.sharh: He has no right to call himself faithful, he says, when he has not shared what befell the one he loved: the beloved lies in the earth and he is still alive. The word for what befell him also means decay, and so answers the body wasting in the line before.

translation: You die, and I do not die of grief for you:
by God, I have betrayed my love for you.
23.sharh: The one he loved has died and he has not died of grief, so he swears he has been a traitor to that love. True faithfulness, for him, would have been to die too.

translation: How ashamed I am when they call me a lover,
and I did nothing for you in the calamity that came.
24.sharh: He is ashamed to be called a lover, since he could do nothing for the beloved when the calamity came. The name, for him, is a claim his deeds never backed.

translation: I see many weeping for you alongside me,
but one who weeps is not like one who makes himself weep.
25.sharh: Many weep with him at the loss, but there is a difference between those who truly grieve and those who only put on a show of tears.

translation: O you who have set out on a distant journey,
when, tell me, do you return from where you went?
26.sharh: He speaks to the dead as to a traveller gone on a long journey, and asks when he will come back. The verb for setting out and the noun for the far place come from one root.

translation: May God reward you for me with every good,
and I know that He has rewarded you for me.
27.sharh: He prays that God reward the dead one on his behalf, then adds that he knows God already has, so the prayer ends in confidence.

translation: O grave of the beloved, I wish
I could carry your earth, even upon my eyes.
28.sharh: He wishes he could carry the grave's earth, even on his eyes. To carry something on one's eyes is the furthest one can go to honour and protect it.

translation: May the rain water you in streams, or if not,
the tears I have watered you with are enough for you.
29.sharh: He asks the rain to water the grave; if it does not, his own tears have watered it enough. Praying for rain on a grave is a custom of Arabic elegy.

translation: And may my greeting of peace never cease to reach you,
fluttering with the breeze over your mound.
30.sharh: He ends with a greeting of peace that never stops, fluttering on the breeze over the grave as a bird beats its wings.

2.2.3-5.meaning: “You do not praise your night journey”: a turn on the proverb “At morning the people praise the night's march”, said of one who bears hardship in hope of rest.

3.2.6.head: عَسى
3.2.6.meaning: “What may you do”: what good can it do you.

5.1.1.meaning: “By my soul”: I would give my soul as his ransom.

9.1.5.meaning: Taraqi: the collarbones. When the soul reaches them, death is at hand.

18.1.1-2.meaning: “It weighs on me”: it grieves me, I can hardly bear it.

18.2.2.meaning: “For your place”: the diwan has “in your place”, searching the spot where you used to be.

19.2.4.head: حُلى
19.2.4.meaning: Hula: adornments; of a person, his looks and bearing.

21.1.1-2.meaning: “Oh, my grief”: a cry of mourning.

22.2.5.head: بَلاء
22.2.5.meaning: Bala': trial, affliction; also decay, the wasting of the body in line 21. Palmer's text has bila, decay.

23.2.1-2.meaning: “By God's right”: an oath. The diwan has “by your love”.

25.2.6.meaning: Made himself weep, put on a show of tears.

26.2.6.head: نَوى
26.2.6.meaning: Nawa: distance; the far place a traveller sets out for.

28.2.5.head: ثَرى
28.2.5.meaning: Thara: moist earth; here the earth of the grave.

30.2.1.head: رَفَّ
30.2.1.meaning: Flutters, as a bird beats its wings. Palmer and the Cairo edition have yariqqu, “grows gentle”.

30.2.5.head: ذُرى
30.2.5.meaning: Dhura: the top of a thing; here the top of the grave mound.
